description.narrative: Den riktningsgivande vision som ICTJ arbetar emot är att "Samhällen bryter cykler av massöverträdelser av mänskliga rättigheter och lägger grunden för fred, rättvisa och inkludering". ICTJ formulerar sitt eget uppdrag som att "Arbeta brett för att utmana grundorsaker och åtgärda konsekvenser av grova MR-överträdelser utifrån offers värdighet, kamp mot straffrihet och genom att främja institutioners ansvarstagande". ICTJ arbetar först och främst med civilsamhällesaktörer, i synnerhet offer för MR-överträdelser, för att stötta dem att få sina rättigheter tillgodosedda i enlighet med egna prioriteringar. ICTJ arbetar dessutom med staten och dess institutioner för att de ska ta sitt ansvar och leverera de rättigheter och åtgärder som främjar upprättelse för offer, rättvisa och långsiktigt hållbar fred. Därutöver arbetar ICTJ på global nivå med policyutveckling inom övergångsrättvisa och driver en förändring mot mer av kontextanpassning och för större tydlighet kring, och erkännande för, den centrala roll övergångsrättvisa har i fredsprocesser och för hållbar fred generellt.

International Center for Transitional Justice (ICTJ) har ansökt hos Sida om 40 miljoner kronor i kärnstöd för genomförande av sin strategiska plan 2018-2022.
ICTJ arbetar för att samhällen skall hantera massiva brott mot mänskliga rättigheter på ett ansvarsfullt och genderkänsligt sätt för att bidra till att undvika förnyad konflikt samt för att främja hållbar fred. För att uppnå detta stödjer ICTJ civilsamhällesaktörer som företräder offer för MR-överträdelser; stärker och främjar medvetenhet och kapacitet hos statliga aktörer och institutioner; samt bidrar till kunskap och policyutveckling på internationell nivå kring övergångsrättvisa.
ICTJ har huvudkontor i New York, landkontor i Colombia, Côte d'Ivoire, Kenya, Libanon (för Syrien), Nepal, Tunisien och Uganda och har därtill engagemang i ytterligare ett antal länder, inklusive Sri Lanka och Gambia.
ICTJ:s totala budget för perioden är cirka 250 miljoner kronor. ICTJ får finansiering från andra institutionella givare, varav Nederländerna är den största bidragsgivaren,och från privata fonder och stiftelser, varav ungefär hälften är öronmärkt, hälften kärnstöd.

International Center for Transitional Justice (ICTJ) has applied to Sida for 40 million SEK to implement their Strategic Plan 2018-2022.
ICTJ's Objective is that Societies implement responsive and gender-sensitive solutions to address legacies of massive human rights violations, which in turn contributes to prevent relapse into violent conflict and to build sustainable peace. To achieve this, ICTJ supports victims' organisations, works with institutions to increase capacity and awareness, and contributes to build knowledge and develop policy at the international level on transitional justice.
ICTJ has its HQ in New York, country offices in Colombia, Côte d'Ivoire, Kenya, Lebanon (for Syria), Nepal, Tunisia and Uganda, and is active in additional countries, including Sri Lanka and The Gambia.
The total budget for ICTJ's operations for the four years is approximately 250 million SEK. Other contributions come from institutional donors, whereof the Netherlands is the main donor, and from private foundations. ICTJ receives about half of their funding as earmarked, and half as core funding.

Over the past agreement period, ICTJ has shown a broad range of relevant results at the local level as well as on a global policy level. Given that this contribution comes from the global strategy for Sustainable Peace to which (global) policy-related outcomes are of particular relevance, selected highlights below do not focus on detailed country-level results but rather on more overall processes, even if illustrated by country-related examples. For the latest annual narrative report (FY22), see Dox 027661/22.
- During the overall agreement period, ICTJ has clearly contributed to an increased level of attention to Transitional Justice (TJ) in the global discourse. ICTJ's advocacy for a more context-specific and inclusive approach to designing TJ solutions, became particularly evident during the first-ever UN Security Council open debate on TJ in February 2020, the planning of which ICTJ contributed to substantially. The debate was attended by 57 countries, experts as well as representatives from ICRC and EU. ICTJ was referred to by several countries during the debate which clearly underlines the key role the organisation play within this field.
- Another overall milestone is ICTJ's publication Transitional Justice and Prevention from 2021, a report that summarises the main findings of a two-year research project drawn from five country case studies: Colombia, Morocco, Peru, the Philippines, and Sierra Leone. The study shows that transitional justice can contribute to sustainable peace and development by preventing human rights violations, as well as different forms of violence, systemic crime, violent conflict, and authoritarianism in various ways, including by addressing common drivers of violence such as exclusion and related grievances at the individual, group, and structural levels, and by catalysing the long-term reform of institutions, laws, and ideologies. It also highlights the importance of inclusive processes, implementation, and political and security contexts.
- Furthermore, the 2022 Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) report to the Human Rights Council (HRC) in January, created with consultations from ICTJ, focuses on transitional justices contributions to sustainable peace and development.The report shows the policy influence of ICTJs approach, messaging, and work in different areas. It specifically references the conclusions of the Working Group on Transitional Justice and SDG16s (led by ICTJ) report On Solid Ground as well as recent ICTJ publications on gender in The Gambia, measuring results, and prevention.
- A more context-specific example is ICTJs work with women victims on the ground in Gambia, which resulted in the only report by women submitted to the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission (TRRC) in The Gambia. The report describes womens experiences during the dictatorship and helped expand the understanding of violations.
Financial year 2022 (April 1 2021 - March 31 2022):
- Quantitative data collected by ICTJs MEL team confirms that over 90% of ICTJ's civil society partners perceive that they improved their ability to pursue justice and demand their rights. When considering survey data disaggregated by gender, women participants tend to provide higher rankings. In this, it is important to consider that a significant proportion of ICTJs activities benefit women, focusing on the role of women in building peace, participating in democracy and in establishing priorities for policies and processes, for example (considering data from this period, women make up over 60% of the total beneficiaries).
- With ICTJs support, their civil society partners were able to produce about 20 different policy proposals, declarations, or reports to engage with processes in their countries and articulate their demands. These included several reports from Colombian civil society partners to inform the work of the Truth Commission and the Special Jurisdiction for Peace as well as Syrian organizations presenting a Guide to Untold Darkness about the situation of the missing and their families.
- Related to gender equality and gender justice, in addition to programmatic work carried out at country level, in March 2022, ICTJ submitted comments to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in response to the the Office of the Prosecutor's launch of a public consultation to inform their new policy initiative to advance accountability for the crime against humanity of persecution on the grounds of gender under the Rome Statue. The initiative, culminating in a comprehensive policy paper, aims to describe and guide the OTP in ensuring a systematic approach to dealing with these crimes. For Sida an the Unit for Peace and Security, this also involves a valuable synergy between contributions as the ICC Trust Fund for Victims is another partner in the portfolio - also very much engaged in gender aspects of its work with reparations, e.g. ICC-related.
- ICTJ continued to engage with children and young people as political actors. In Mali for example, as the Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission (CVJR) was concluding its work, ICTJ helped reviewing, upon request from UNICEF, the childrens chapter of the CVJRs final report and develop a methodology to produce a child and youth friendly version, as well as how to involve young people in the development of the report.
- Related to work focused on combating corruption, examples from the past year include work in Tunisia where 'dictatorship-era' corruption has been a unique feature of its transitional justice process and where ICTJ monitored the corruption cases dealt with by the Specialized Chambers. In Armenia, where the post-2018 revolution government adopted anti-corruption as a priority, ICTJ has advocated for addressing corruption as part of a comprehensive transitional justice strategy. In June 2021, ICTJ also held an online roundtable discussion with media professionals from the region to discuss the role of the media in addressing the interrelationship between corruption, conflict, and democratization. In addition, in December 2021, ICTJ organized an online panel discussion with youth, victims, civil society, and policymakers to address corruption, human rights abuses, and institutional reforms.
- Related to the portion of funding labeled as 'flexible funds' (see also under the section below on lessons learned for future interventions), ICTJ ICTJ responded to ad hoc requests for analysis and technical assistance to domestic and international stakeholders as well as monitored developments in amonbg others South Sudan, Georgia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Ukraine. A concrete example is training provided to the Technical Committee related to the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan (R-ARCSS)on TJ concepts and best practices, the transitional justice requirements of the R-ARCSS, methodologies for consultations with a national scope, principles for establishing an effective truth commission, stakeholder mapping techniques, internal management and accountability tools, and ways to conduct outreach.
For more details, a separate account for the 'flexible funds' has been submitted, see Dox 027661/22.
